newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bonds subdued, await first U.S. test.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds subdued, await first U.S. test.

text.p: *Australian bonds saw very little action as the market awaited the first of this week's key data from the U.S. -- the first quarter employment index.
*Major local data not due until tail end of week.

The Australian bond market saw very little action as it waited to sift through the first of several key U.S. indicators this week with the release of the first quarter employment costs index later on Tuesday.

"We've seen very little physical activity, and anything that has been done has been through the futures market," one trader said. "The feeling is we won't be trading at this sort of levels on Monday after the (U.S.) payrolls numbers."
The local market has very little to trade off on the domestic front until Thursday's average weekly oridinary time earnings and retail trade.
"If they turn out weak, you could see the market start to build in the possibility of a rate cut again," the trader added.

The local market had rallied strongly last week after the moderate outcome to the "living wage" claim case, but subsequently sold off on profit-taking, having been seen to be overzealous in predicting the first quarter inflation report, even though it still turned out to be benign.

However, the immediate focus is on the U.S., and whether this week's data will add to expectations that the Federal Open Market Committee will endorse a further tightening in the Fed funds rate on May 20.

The U.S. employment costs index at 1230 GMT is expected to have risen 0.9 percent in the first quarter after the 0.8 percent increase in the fourth quarter last year, according to a Reuters survey of economists.
A reading of 1.0 percent or above is expected to be taken bearishly by the market.
Meanwhile, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan is due to address the International Monetary Fund/World Bank spring meeting in Washington at 1630 GMT.

Spread differentials to the U.S. widened slightly during the day, but remained tighter to Canada amid a vulnerable Canadian dollar ahead of the June 2 Canadian election. Long New Zealand debt put in a strong rally, which traders there linked to the unwinding of recent curve steepening trades.
